summary: Submits an idea for using IP and ARP on mixed FDDI networks that contain both single-MAC and dual-MAC stations, by introducing a new protocol layer. It is informational and offers a proposal, not a standard.

eli5.summary: Some stations on a ring network are built differently and cannot find each other easily. This paper suggests an extra helper step so they can.

questions: how does arp work on dual mac fddi
what is a dual mac fddi station
what is the load sharing layer in fddi
subtitle: A proposal for a load sharing layer that lets dual MAC FDDI stations use both rings while ARP and IP stay unchanged.

tldr.problem: On an FDDI network that mixes single MAC and dual MAC stations, ARP only knows one hardware address per station, so dual MAC stations cannot easily use both rings.
tldr.mechanism: A new load sharing layer sits under ARP and IP in dual MAC stations. It uses a small protocol, DMARP, to swap secondary MAC addresses on the secondary ring, and it keeps an address cache that decides which ring each IP frame uses.
tldr.outcome: Two dual MAC stations could share load across both rings and use 200 Mbits/s, with no change to single MAC stations or transparent bridges. The memo is an informational idea, not a standard.

facts.label: DMARP operations
facts.value: 7 (reply, request, error, search, found, query, hold)

today: RFC 1329 is an Informational RFC that offers an idea and does not specify a standard. It has been updated by RFC 5494.

sections.title: Dual MAC Stations on FDDI
sections.content:
An FDDI network can have a primary and a secondary ring. A single MAC station attaches one MAC (media access controller) to the primary ring. A dual MAC station has two: a primary MAC (P-MAC) and a secondary MAC (S-MAC), each with its own address as the FDDI SMT standard requires.

RFC 1329 calls a ring with both kinds of station an inhomogeneous ring. Its idea is that two dual MAC stations can split their traffic across both rings and use the double bandwidth of 200 Mbits/s, as single MAC stations cannot.

The RFC makes some assumptions. When the dual ring wraps, both MACs of a dual MAC station are assumed to stay connected. Single MAC stations are assumed to sit on the primary ring. Transparent bridges may join rings, but none are allowed between a primary and a secondary ring.
sections.eli5: Some computers on the ring have two doors into the network and some have one. The note asks how the two-door computers can use both doors.

sections.title: The Load Sharing Layer
sections.content:
In single MAC stations, IP and ARP run over SNAP and 802.2 LLC type 1 (connectionless). Dual MAC stations get a new load sharing layer between ARP/IP and two SNAP/LLC/MAC stacks, one per ring. It offers ARP the same interface that SNAP does, so the property "dual MAC" is transparent to ARP, IP and higher layers.

The load sharing entity has three parts: the address cache, the cache administration and the multiplexer. The cache holds primary and secondary MAC addresses for other dual MAC stations only, never for single MAC stations.
sections.eli5: A new helper layer sits between the computer's normal software and the two doors. The normal software never has to know there are two.

sections.title: Learning Addresses with DMARP
sections.content:
ARP only learns primary MAC addresses, because the load sharing layer always sends ARP frames over the primary ring. To learn secondary addresses, dual MAC stations use the Dual MAC Address Resolution Protocol (DMARP). Every time an ARP frame goes out on the primary ring, a DMARP reply carrying the station's primary and secondary MAC addresses goes out on the secondary ring, addressed to the broadcast MAC address.

If two dual MAC stations sit on different dual rings joined by one transparent bridge, they cannot share load. A cache entry for such a station gets the OR-bit ("other ring"), and no load sharing is done with it. A timer later sends a DMARP request to the secondary MAC and discards the entry, so the entry can be learned again if the network changed.

On large networks, rings are more likely to be wrapped while stations first meet. The RFC adds extra control bits to cope: a read-only R-bit for manually written entries, a Hold bit (H) that marks load sharing as trusted and is re-checked by query and hold frames, and search and found frames that let a third station help two others.
sections.eli5: While two computers say hello the normal way, they also whisper their second door number on the other road. If they turn out to live on different rings, they skip the second road.

sections.title: Address Cache and DMARP Frames
sections.content:
Each cache entry holds a 48-bit P-MAC address, a 48-bit S-MAC address, and bits LS (load sharing possible), OR, H, Q (query sent), R (read-only) and V (valid), plus a 32-bit subscript and a 16-bit protocol type. LS and OR always have inverted values, so one is redundant, but both are defined to make state checks easier.

DMARP frames reuse the ARP layout: hardware type, protocol type (2048 for the Internet Protocol), the two address lengths, a 16-bit operation field, then two hardware addresses and the sender and receiver protocol addresses. They travel in a SNAP header with OUI zero and a new EtherType that the RFC says is not yet defined.

Apart from error frames, all DMARP frames go on the secondary ring. Reply, error and search frames use the broadcast hardware address. Request, found, query and hold frames go to an individual secondary MAC address.
sections.eli5: The whisper message looks like a normal ARP message with a number saying what kind of whisper it is, such as a reply, a question or a search.

sections.title: Multiplexer and Timers
sections.content:
The multiplexer decides which ring carries each outgoing IP frame. Broadcast and multicast frames always go on the primary ring, because a single MAC station might be a target. If there is no cache entry for the destination, or the LS-bit is not set, the frame also goes on the primary ring. Otherwise a load sharing criterion chooses the ring. The RFC leaves the criterion open and gives transmit queue length as an example. Multicast and broadcast frames received from the secondary MAC are discarded to avoid duplicates.

Three timers are used per cache entry: OR-Entry-Timer, Hold-Timer and Query-Timer. The RFC suggests about 10 seconds for OR-set-timeout and several minutes for Hold-time and Query-time, all longer than a frame needs to cross the whole network.
sections.eli5: A traffic officer sends each message down the second road only if the other computer is known to have a second door. Party announcements always take the main road so nobody hears them twice.

viz.caption: PROTOCOL LAYERS IN A DUAL MAC STATION (RFC 1329)

items.label: reply
items.desc: Announces primary and secondary MAC addresses; broadcast.

items.label: request
items.desc: Asks a station to send a reply; sent to its secondary MAC.

items.label: error
items.desc: Guards against a lost reply; broadcast.

items.label: search
items.desc: Asks whether a third station can arrange load sharing; broadcast.

items.label: found
items.desc: Third station reports a sure load sharing; to a secondary MAC.

items.label: query
items.desc: Checks that the Hold bit is still correct; to a secondary MAC.

items.label: hold
items.desc: Acknowledges a query; to a secondary MAC.
